subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease diagnosis and IVIG timing in a 2 year old
stem: A 2-year-old girl has had 6 days of fever to 40 degrees C despite two courses of amoxicillin, with 3 days of rash, cracked bleeding lips and a strawberry tongue. No conjunctivitis or lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: Irritable, oedematous dorsum of both hands and feet
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L, platelets 620 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, albumin 24 g/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Lumbar puncture with intravenous vancomycin and cefotaxime
options.rationale: No meningitic signs are present and CSF cell counts are not part of Kawasaki work-up; broad-spectrum antibiotics do not treat the underlying vasculitis (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: Continue amoxicillin and add roxithromycin for atypical cover
options.rationale: Prolonged fever unresponsive to antibiotics with mucocutaneous features and inflammatory markers is not treated by broader antibiotics; missing Kawasaki risks coronary aneurysm (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: Paracetamol for symptom control, reassessing after 48 hours
options.rationale: Symptomatic management alone in Kawasaki disease allows the coronary artery aneurysm window to close beyond 10 days when IVIG efficacy falls sharply (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement).

options.text: Echocardiography with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin
options.rationale: She meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria (fever 5 days plus 2 of 5 principal features with supportive labs: CRP high, platelets high, albumin low, ALT high, sterile pyuria and anaemia); IVIG plus aspirin is indicated and echocardiogram baselines coronary artery status (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: High dose oral prednisolone monotherapy for 14 days
options.rationale: Oral steroids are used as an adjunct in high risk patients such as the Kobayashi score high risk group or IVIG resistant disease; steroid monotherapy is not first-line in AU (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement).

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis of childhood whose only preventable morbidity is coronary artery aneurysm; IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. Complete criteria require fever at least 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features (conjunctivitis, rash, lips or oral mucosal changes, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete disease is diagnosed with fever plus fewer principal features when supportive laboratory features are present, and treatment is unchanged. High dose aspirin is anti-inflammatory during the acute phase then low-dose aspirin continues for coronary risk.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 to under 5 percent
Incomplete Kawasaki meets criteria with fewer features plus lab support
High dose aspirin for anti-inflammatory effect, then low-dose
Efficacy of IVIG falls sharply beyond 10 days of fever
explanation.pearls: The Kobayashi score identifies IVIG-resistant Japanese children; it is not calibrated in Australian populations but a high score triggers steroid coprescription with IVIG in high risk cases.

subtopic_detail: first line management of a persistent infant head tilt with restricted neck rotation
stem: A 9-week-old boy has tipped his head towards the right shoulder since three weeks of age and prefers to look left. He was born at term by forceps delivery and feeds well.

data_table.Examination: Right head tilt with left chin rotation, firm non-tender mass in the right sternocleidomastoid, passive right rotation limited to 50 degrees, right occipital flattening, hips abduct fully

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the tilt is of later onset, painful, or accompanied by abnormal neurology, abnormal eye movements or a fixed bony deformity, none of which apply. A normal neurological and ocular examination with a palpable muscle mass makes a structural cause very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure and review at his twelve month check
options.rationale: Positional preference with full passive range does resolve spontaneously, but this infant has a genuine restriction of passive rotation, which does not. Waiting until twelve months moves him past the window in which stretching is most effective. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for stretching and positioning
options.rationale: Restricted passive rotation with a palpable sternocleidomastoid mass in an otherwise normal infant is congenital muscular torticollis, and supervised stretching started before three months of age resolves the great majority without surgery. The plagiocephaly is positional and corrects as rotation is regained. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Ultrasound both hips before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Hip dysplasia is associated with congenital muscular torticollis, but a clinical hip examination that is fully normal at this age is the screen, and imaging is added only if the examination is abnormal or other risk factors are present. This would delay the treatment that actually changes outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Fit a cranial remoulding orthosis for the flattening
options.rationale: A helmet addresses the secondary skull shape and not the shortened muscle that is causing it, and it is considered only after several months of failed repositioning and physiotherapy. Treating the cause first usually makes the orthosis unnecessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis usually presents in the first two months as a head tilt towards a shortened sternocleidomastoid with the chin rotated away, often with a palpable fibrous mass within the muscle. The key examination finding is restriction of passive rotation and contralateral lateral flexion, which distinguishes it from a simple positional preference in which passive range is full. Secondary deformational plagiocephaly develops because the infant consistently rests on the same part of the skull, and it improves once rotation is restored. Outcomes depend strongly on how early physiotherapy begins, with treatment started before three months resolving the deformity in the large majority of infants. Ocular causes, cervical spine anomalies and posterior fossa lesions should be considered when the tilt is late in onset, painful, or accompanied by abnormal neurology.
key_points: Restricted passive rotation separates muscular torticollis from positional head preference
A palpable sternocleidomastoid mass is present in a substantial minority and is not a tumour
Deformational plagiocephaly is secondary and corrects as the neck restriction resolves
Physiotherapy started before three months of age gives the best resolution rates
Abnormal eye movements, pain or abnormal neurology mandate imaging rather than physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Every infant with congenital muscular torticollis needs a careful hip examination at the same visit, because developmental dysplasia of the hip coexists in roughly one in five and both conditions share the same intrauterine crowding mechanism.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
